why: It is an LIS-style DP over increasing subsequences, but each state stores a set instead of a length: S[v] = the set of OR scores of increasing subsequences ending with value v. Since values are below 1024, each set is a 1024-bit mask, and a Fenwick tree over values gives the union of S[u] for all u < x.
hints: Values are below 1024, so every OR score is also below 1024: the answer is just a subset of 0..1023.

Like LIS, process the array left to right; a subsequence ending at x extends any increasing subsequence ending in a smaller value. Track, for each ending value, the set of reachable OR scores as a bitmask.

Query a Fenwick tree (OR of masks) for values < x, transform every score s into s | x, add x alone, and write back at x. Collect everything plus 0 for the empty subsequence. O(n log V) mask operations.
pitfalls: The empty subsequence counts and scores 0 (see the expected [0,...]).
Strictly increasing: equal values cannot chain, so query values strictly less than x.
Brute-forcing subsequences is exponential; even O(n^2 * 1024) is too slow for n = 10^4.
